title: Wearable-Derived Heart Rate Variability Across the Menstrual Cycle, Hormonal Contraceptive Use, and Reproductive Life Stages in Females: A Living Systematic Review
authors: de Jager E, Caulfield B, Angelidi E, MacNamee B, Holden S
population: Females of any age in 16 studies of wearable- or mobile-measured HRV across the menstrual cycle, hormonal contraceptive use or reproductive life stage
findings: 16 studies included from 299 records (search to December 2025); evidence quality moderate (Newcastle-Ottawa 7/9).
In naturally menstruating females, HRV was higher at the beginning of the cycle and lower toward the end, with time-domain HRV differences of 3 to 9%.
Hormonal contraceptive users exhibited lower HRV, particularly in the late cycle; HRV tended to decline after menopause with increasing age.
Inconsistent phase and menopause classification prevented quantitative synthesis; authors state this should be considered when presenting HRV metrics to female users.
limitations: No pooling; HRV only, not performance or training decisions. Whether a 3-9% cyclic change alters training decisions was not tested.
implications: Compare each female user with her own rolling HRV baseline and widen the alert band so a within-cycle drop of 3-9% is not flagged as stress by itself (the range is observed, not a validated correction factor).
Show a caveat on HRV trends for female and hormonal-contraceptive users; never auto-reduce load on one low late-cycle reading.
Use a baseline window of at least one full cycle (about 28-35 days) for female users (design default, not stated by the authors).

verification.notes: Crossref matches (Sports Med, online 2026-01, de Jager). Numbers confirmed in Europe PMC abstract (PMID 41545627). Evidence level lowered A to B: moderate quality, no pooling.
